articles.title: How the body clock could help personalise depression treatment
articles.author: Timothy Hearn, Lecturer, University of Cambridge; Anglia Ruskin University
articles.summary: A new study suggests that sleep patterns may be linked to how people respond to antidepressants, raising the possibility of more personalised treatment.
articles.contentHtml:
A person with depression might sleep much longer than usual and still wake feeling exhausted. Later that evening, when they want to go to bed, they may find themselves wide awake. Researchers are investigating whether patterns like these could help explain why antidepressants work better for some people than others.

The clue may lie in the body’s internal clock, which helps regulate when someone sleeps, wakes and feels alert.

An Australian study examined 11,380 people, predominantly with severe or recurring depression. About 23% met the researchers’ criteria for a proposed subtype called “circadian depression”, named after the body’s roughly 24-hour internal clock.

Participants needed at least three of six features, including being a night owl, sleeping longer during depression, morning tiredness and seasonal changes in mood or behaviour. The other features involved habitually sleeping and waking later, and having different sleep schedules on working days and days off.

Compared with other participants, this group reported less benefit and more side-effects from two common types of antidepressants, SSRIs and SNRIs, which affect how brain cells communicate through chemical messengers. However, some people with these sleep patterns still reported benefiting from these medicines.

The researchers also found genetic associations with later sleep timing, reduced sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar, and a protein involved in inflammation, the immune system’s response to injury or infection. These associations reflect inherited tendencies, rather than evidence that participants actually had blood-sugar problems or inflammation.

The findings are preliminary. Participants recalled their symptoms and medication experiences, and those in the proposed group generally had more severe depression. The researchers did not measure their internal clocks or establish cause and effect.

Some features overlap with recognised forms of depression, so it remains unclear whether this is a distinct subtype. All participants had European genetic ancestry, limiting how widely the findings can be applied. The 23% figure therefore cannot be assumed to represent everyone with depression.

How the body clock affects mood

The body clock coordinates roughly 24-hour cycles, known as circadian rhythms, which affect sleepiness, body temperature and hormones, the chemical messengers that help regulate the body. Light reaching the eyes helps keep this clock aligned with day and night. Meals and physical activity also provide timing cues.

When internal timing clashes with daily demands, sleep can suffer. Someone whose clock runs late may feel alert at midnight but have to get up for work while their body is still expecting sleep. Being a night owl is not necessarily a problem. Persistent disruption is the concern.

Sleep and mental health can reinforce one another. Disrupted sleep may worsen depression, while depression and stress can disturb sleep and daily routines.

One possible link involves brain systems that regulate emotion and reward, including the ability to enjoy pleasurable experiences. Animal experiments suggest that disrupting the body clock can affect these systems and produce depression-like behaviour.

In small laboratory experiments, researchers altered the sleep schedules of shift workers and people who did not work shifts. When their sleep and waking times were out of step with their internal clocks, participants reported worse mood. They had not been recruited because they had depression, and temporary low mood is different from clinical depression.

Conventional antidepressants might leave a timing problem untreated, but that remains a hypothesis. The Australian study did not test body-clock treatments, and its findings cannot establish whether someone with disrupted rhythms would benefit more from an alternative medication.

Could light therapy help?

Light therapy involves sitting near a specially designed bright-light box at a scheduled time, often in the morning. Morning light can shift a late-running body clock earlier, helping someone feel sleepy and wake earlier.

Read more: Why morning blue light therapy could improve sleep and daily activity in older adults

The treatment is used for seasonal affective disorder, depression that follows a seasonal pattern, often during darker months. Evidence suggests it can also help with depression that has no seasonal pattern.

A review of 11 clinical trials involving 858 people examined bright-light therapy for non-seasonal depression, including bipolar depression. Bipolar disorder involves depression alongside episodes of unusually elevated or irritable mood and increased energy.

In trials reporting remission, about 41% of people receiving bright light improved enough to fall below the threshold for depression, compared with 24% receiving dim light or treatment without bright light.

But these trials did not select people with the proposed circadian subtype, so they cannot tell us whether that group benefits more. Light may also influence mood through brain pathways separate from the body clock.

Timing and medical guidance matter. Light can shift the clock earlier or later depending on when it is used. People with bipolar disorder need particular supervision because light therapy can sometimes trigger unusually elevated or irritable mood.

Regular waking times, daytime activity and meals may also support daily rhythms. Melatonin, a hormone that rises in the evening and signals biological night, can help shift a delayed clock when carefully timed. However, studies have not established melatonin supplements as an effective depression treatment.

Towards more personalised treatment

Could measuring someone’s internal clock help doctors choose treatments? Wrist-worn activity monitors can estimate sleep patterns, while saliva samples taken throughout an evening can show when melatonin starts rising, offering a more direct measure of internal timing.

Researchers need to establish whether the proposed group really has distinct biological rhythms, then test whether choosing treatment based on those measurements helps people recover sooner.

For now, sleep patterns cannot reliably predict which antidepressant will work best, and the findings provide no reason to change prescribed medication without medical advice.

If future trials confirm a benefit, a prescription for depression might one day specify when to receive light as carefully as which medicine to take.

articles.title: Spending in-person time with friends is the biggest predictor of whether college students flourish
articles.author: Roxanne Prichard, Professor of Psychology, University of St. Thomas
articles.summary: Helping young people thrive involves supporting healthy relationships, as well as being engaged in work, school and family life.
articles.contentHtml:
Exercise, avoiding alcohol or even getting enough sleep aren’t the factors most connected to college students’ well-being.

Spending face-to-face time with friends and other people is the strongest predictor of their mental health, according to a 2026 study of nearly 80,000 students that I conducted with the help of my students.

This finding matters because young people are spending less time together in person and more time communicating through screens.

Between 2010 and 2022, the percentage of U.S. high school seniors who reported seeing friends face-to-face almost every day declined from 44% to 32%.

Against this backdrop, mental health challenges among young people have become an increasing public health concern.

Suicide remains the second-leading cause of death among Americans ages 15 to 34.

But mental health is about more than the absence of mental illness. My student researchers and I wanted to ask a somewhat different question: What helps young people flourish?

To answer that question, we created a broad measure of well-being that captured more than the lack of mental health problems, such as psychological distress. It also included positive aspects of life, such as having supportive relationships, hobbies and a sense of meaning and purpose.

A range of measures to determine well-being

Our research team analyzed responses from 79,246 college students across the United States and Canada.

We examined 51 aspects of students’ lives, including their substance use, the discrimination they encountered, their financial stress, any sleep problems and different relationship challenges.

We also examined how students spent their free time, whether that meant exercising, studying, socializing, meditating, playing video games or scrolling on social media.

We used statistical methods that allowed us to compare dozens of potential influences on student well-being simultaneously, helping us identify which factors were most strongly associated with flourishing.

Among the dozens of factors we examined, six stood out as the most important and influential.

Time spent with others pays off

The strongest factor connected to student flourishing was remarkably ordinary: spending time with other people. Students who spent more hours socializing with friends, attending student organizations and participating in cultural events tended to report feeling an overall sense of well-being.

The second most important factor surprised us. Students who spent more time on obligations, including paid work and unpaid family responsibilities, also tended to report a greater sense of well-being.

Our results raise an intriguing possibility: Well-being may come not only from leisure and self-care but also from contributing to something larger than oneself.

While problematic substance use, passive screen time and sleep problems tended to compromise well-being, these factors weren’t the biggest detriment. It was difficulty navigating interpersonal relationships, including problems with friends, romantic partners and roommates.

Making friends, maintaining healthy relationships and working through conflicts requires practice, and some of that practice time now competes with communication mediated by screens.

Notably, the contributors to student flourishing were similar among students diagnosed with anxiety or depression and those without these diagnoses. That suggests these everyday experiences may matter across a broad spectrum of mental health.

Helping students thrive

Supporting students’ mental and emotional health is not simply a matter of reducing screen time. It also means making it easier for young people to spend time together in person, whether through clubs, recreation programs, community events or other welcoming spaces.

Counseling and educational programs can likewise help students build friendships, communicate effectively and navigate conflict in healthy ways.

None of this means mental illness can be solved by telling a struggling young person to put down their phone, join a club or get more sleep. Mental health conditions are complex, and people experiencing them need access to effective professional care.

But our findings suggest that helping young people thrive requires more than treating symptoms. It also requires cultivating supportive relationships, healthy sleep and meaningful engagement in work, school and family life.

Roxanne Prichard receives funding from the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Five ways to look after yourself as winter approaches
articles.author: Andy M Morley, Subject Lead: Psychology & Neuroscience, University of Lancashire
articles.summary: A few small changes to your daily routine can help you cope better during the winter months.
articles.contentHtml:
When the clocks “fall back” in the autumn, it signals the start of the winter months. And, for many, this time change also signals the start of a difficult period – where the cold weather and long nights wear on their mental health.

To help you adjust to the darker evenings, here are our five top tips for easing your way through the winter:

1. Make the most of the daylight

Natural light regulates our body clock – the internal system which influences our sleep quality and alertness. Your body will take time to adjust to the changes, notably the evenings being darker, earlier. This in turn may disrupt your sleep patterns, which might mean grumpier mornings due to a lack of sleep.

Try to make the most of the day’s light by spending time outdoors – even if this is just a walk around the block during your lunch or while on a coffee break. A change of scenery can offer a welcome pause from the pressures of everyday life and help you feel refreshed, particularly if you focus on the greenery around you.

Even if you cannot find time to leave the building, try sitting next by a window to enjoy some natural light and a different perspective on you surroundings.

2. Keep moving

When it’s cold and dark, it’s all too easy to skip your workouts and hunker down inside with a hot drink or favourite snack instead.

But exercise has many benefits for us beyond just the physical ones. It can reduce stress and improve your mental health.

Taking a stroll, visiting the gym or even walking laps around your kitchen table or garden will help you cope with the change in the season. You could even combine exercise with seasonal activities – such as walking to see Halloween decorations or Christmas lights in the local area.

3. Be kind to yourself

It’s perfectly okay to adjust your expectations about your daily accomplishments in the winter months. With less daylight and worsening weather it can be hard to keep to the pace of life you’ve set yourself and enjoyed over the summer months.

Self-compassion supports your wellbeing. This can involve being kind to yourself, recognising the things you have achieved and celebrating the small wins along the way.

You don’t have to make the most of everyday, or be productive all of the time. Find the balance and allow yourself some slower days. And rather than criticising yourself for not completing everything you had lined up for the day, acknowledge what you have achieved. Having this kind of self-compassion is linked with better mental wellbeing.

4. Stay connected to others

When it’s dark, cold and wet, it’s easy to want to prioritise “me time” at the expense of catching up. But making time for your friends and family is key during the winter months. This is because strong social connections are important for good mental health.

Even if it’s just a short chat about a new film you’ve seen or a great book you’ve read, this time spent connecting with loved ones and maintaining these meaningful connections can help to support your mental wellbeing.

5. Enjoy life’s simple pleasures

Make time for the little things in life – whether that’s reading, cooking, listening to music or picking up a hobby you forgot about.

Research on behavioural activation, which involves reconnecting with rewarding and meaningful activities, shows that these kinds of endeavours improve mood – particularly when motivation has fallen.

Planning one “fun” thing to do each day – no matter how big or small – can help ease the darker evenings and colder nights. You can also make the most of the longer evenings by snuggling up under the duvet to watch a box set without feeling you have to make the most of being outside, or enjoy more at-home activities – such as cooking a favourite meal or indulging in seasonal treats.

Looking ahead

If nothing else, remember the shortest day of the year (in the UK at least) is only a few weeks away. After that, the evenings will start to get lighter again.

Looking after your mental health during winter isn’t about forcing yourself to be positive – it’s about finding the small ways that provide you with support, happiness or enable you to connect with other people.

Feeling less energetic during the winter is common, but if you have persistent low mood, a loss of interest in activities, feel hopeless or loss your appetite, seek additional support via the NHS. Self-care is important, but you do not have to manage everything alone.

articles.title: Seeing a psychologist is becoming more unequal – and our map shows the gap
articles.author: Danusha Jayawardana, Research Fellow in Health Economics, Monash University
articles.summary: Medicare rebates are meant to make psychologist visits cheaper and more accessible. But data shows those on the lowest incomes are missing out.
articles.contentHtml:
When you’re struggling with your mental health, visiting your GP for a mental health treatment plan can be an important first step.

These plans indicate a diagnosed mental health condition (such as depression or anxiety) and allow you to access up to ten subsidised psychotherapy (or “talk therapy”) sessions through Medicare’s Better Access Initiative.

But what happens next?

Our recently published research suggests whether you actually see a psychologist may depend on where you live.

We found those living in low-income neighourhoods were much less likely to receive psychological care soon after receiving a plan, compared to those in wealthier neighbourhoods.

And in the decade between 2014–23, this gap widened substantially – particularly for children.

Even with subsidies, mental health care can be expensive

While private psychologists can choose their own rate, the suggested fee for a 45–60 minute consultation is A$330. But the Medicare rebate is set at $149.05 for a clinical psychologist – and even less for general psychologists – meaning the gap you pay can be substantial.

Read more: Need to see a psychologist? How to find one that’s right for you

High out-of-pocket costs, long waits and limited local services can prevent people from getting the care they need.

In the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ 2024–25 Patient Experience Survey, about one in four people who needed to see a psychologist reported delaying or going without care because of the cost.

Financial barriers to mental health care were more common in disadvantaged areas.

What we did and what we found

We wanted to understand how large the income-related gaps in psychological care are across Australia.

We used de-identified tax and Medicare data to study 5.4 million Australians who received a GP mental health treatment plan between 2014 and 2023, to look at whether they went on to receive Medicare-subsidised psychotherapy (talk therapy) within three months.

This included services delivered by eligible psychologists, social workers and occupational therapists.

In one study of adults, we found substantial regional differences in access: in 2023, psychotherapy use within three months of receiving a GP mental health treatment plan ranged from approximately 28% in parts of regional New South Wales and South Australia to 60% in inner Perth.

But we also wanted to look at whether income-related gaps had changed over time, and whether children are affected differently from adults.

In another, related study, we looked separately at children under 18 and adults aged 25–54, and compared neighbourhoods with different average incomes.

In 2023, only 32% of children in the lowest-income neighbourhoods received psychotherapy within three months of receiving their plan, compared with 55% in the highest-income neighbourhoods. For adults, the figures were 40% versus 55%.

The gap has widened

A decade earlier, rates of psychotherapy use were higher across the country and the income-related gaps were smaller.

In 2014, 56% of children and 53% of adults in the lowest-income neighbourhoods received psychotherapy within three months of getting a plan. This compared to 70% of children and 61% of adults in the highest-income neighbourhoods.

Over the following decade, uptake fell across all groups – but more steeply in low-income neighbourhoods.

As a result, the income gap widened, especially for children. The divide grew particularly sharply during the COVID pandemic.

Among children in the lowest-income neighbourhoods, the proportion receiving timely psychotherapy fell from more than half (56%) in 2014 to around one-third (32%) in 2023.

We also find a growing “reverse” pattern for medication. Lower-income people are increasingly likely to receive antidepressants without psychotherapy, suggesting a shift toward lower-cost treatment pathways.

This is concerning, especially for children, for whom psychiatric medication without psychotherapy is not typically recommended.

What’s behind this widening gap?

We checked whether the widening income gap could be explained by an increase in diagnoses of complex conditions, such as ADHD and autism, or by the rapid expansion of telehealth in 2020.

But when we analysed these factors separately, the income gap remained – whether or not people had also seen a psychiatrist or paediatrician for a complex condition, and whether they’d received psychotherapy via telehealth or face-to-face.

Rising costs are a more plausible explanation. Between 2014 and 2023, the average out-of-pocket cost of a first therapy session rose from about $44 to $90 for children, and from $35 to $80 for adults. These amounts are adjusted for inflation and expressed in 2023 dollars.

The price increases are consistent with demand for mental health care growing faster than providers’ capacity to offer appointments, particularly during the COVID pandemic.

When demand outpaces supply, waiting times can lengthen and fees can rise. People on lower incomes have less capacity to absorb these higher costs.

Expanding capacity takes time. Training new psychologists takes years, while shifting psychologists from other sectors may create shortages elsewhere.

Read more: Australia has an ongoing GP shortage. Why can’t we just train more GPs?

The regional differences we observed also point to uneven access: where psychologists work matters, as well as how many there are.

So, what would actually help?

Reducing out-of-pocket costs should be a priority. This could include increasing Medicare rebates, introducing targeted subsidies for low-income families, or expanding low-fee and no-gap service models.

Bulk billing may also have a role. Recent reforms have strengthened incentives for GPs to bulk bill, particularly in regional and rural areas. A similar approach could be considered for psychological services, though we need to first carefully evaluate whether these GP reforms have worked.

Improving access will also require building a bigger workforce. Expanding training places, addressing bottlenecks in supervised placements, and supporting early-career psychologists could help increase capacity while maintaining high standards of training and clinical care.

In rural and regional areas, this could mean targeted programs to attract and retain psychologists where shortages are greatest. These could include extra funding for providers in those areas, relocation payments, or waiving higher education loans.

For people with milder symptoms, lower-intensity options such as guided digital therapy or suitable group programs may help reduce pressure on individual therapy services.

Read more: How does Medicare’s new Mental Health Check In work? Is this low-intensity CBT likely to help?

Ultimately, Medicare-subsidised psychotherapy was designed to make mental health care more accessible. Our findings show access has declined and become less equal.

Reforms should prioritise reversing this decline for people in low-income neighbourhoods, especially children.

Danusha Jayawardana receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

David Johnston receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

Nicole Black receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

articles.title: How can African schools support children’s mental health? Research shows what works and what doesn’t
articles.author: Lydia Namatende-Sakwa, Associate Research Scientist, African Population and Health Research Center
articles.summary: Mental health should be treated as part of education quality, learner safety and inclusion.
articles.contentHtml:
Schools are often among the first places where emotional and behavioural difficulties become visible. Learners may start missing classes, withdrawing from friends or struggling academically.

Schools are strategically positioned for mental health intervention because of their centrality in the lives of children and adolescents. They are an important entry point for mental health responsive action that can reach large numbers of children and adolescents through existing systems.

The burden of child and adolescent mental health is especially urgent in Africa for three reasons. First, specialist mental health services are limited. Second, children face a combination of social, economic, health and humanitarian risks. And third, the continent has a young population. In 2024, 46% of Africa’s population were children under 18.

Evidence from high-income countries suggests that comprehensive mental health interventions involving schools, families and communities can improve mental health, social functioning, learning and general wellbeing.

We are part of a research team, Education and Youth Empowerment, that examines inclusive and quality education in Africa, with a focus on school mental health, gender and adolescent well-being. We recently carried out a review of school-based and school-linked strategies aimed at strengthening capacity to address mental health among children and adolescents. Our study screened 1,759 records and 122 scholarly studies that met our criteria.

Among our main findings were these:

  • Promising evidence that brief, structured programmes that teach coping, emotional and problem-solving skills can reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety and improve well-being when delivered by trained non-specialists.

  • Counselling on its own is not enough to prevent mental health problems or address the wider school, family and social conditions that contribute to learners’ distress.

  • Teachers can play an important role in promoting wellbeing, recognising signs of distress and helping learners access support, but they should not be expected to diagnose or treat mental health conditions.

  • Support needs to extend beyond the school to include families, communities, health services and child-protection systems.

  • Schools need to be part of a wider mental health support system, rather than relying on stand-alone services such as counselling rooms, one-off programmes or individual guidance teachers.

This evidence was geographically uneven. Most studies came from a relatively small number of countries, particularly Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, South Africa and Kenya. Evidence was much more limited from francophone and lusophone Africa, north and central Africa, and from rural, remote, pastoralist and conflict-affected settings.

Our findings point to the need for school mental health systems that combine prevention, early identification, teacher support, family and community engagement, and clear referral pathways to specialist care.

What’s working

Our review found promising evidence for brief, structured interventions delivered by trained non-specialists. These include Shamiri, a four-week group intervention tested in Kenyan secondary schools. Under this programme, students meet in small groups for an hour each week, taking part in exercises such as problem-solving, reflecting on personal growth and writing gratitude letters. The sessions are led by trained lay facilitators.

In a trial involving 413 adolescents, participants showed greater reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms than those in a study-skills programme. Benefits were still evident seven months later.

Other promising approaches included:

  • improving mental health awareness among learners and staff to recognise signs of distress, understand mental health, reduce stigma, and know when and where to seek help

  • trained teachers, school staff or peer facilitators building skills such as emotional regulation, empathy, relationships and problem-solving, while enabling young people to support one another

  • using games, music, dance, creative activities and physical movement to support emotional wellbeing, social connection and coping.

An approach employed among refugee children in Uganda combines movement, games, dance, breathing exercises and group activities. Evidence points to improvements in wellbeing and social connectedness, with benefits for traumatic stress and bullying.

These approaches show that school mental health does not have to mean therapy.

Why counselling isn’t enough

Counselling is one of the most common school-based mental health approaches. It provides a confidential space where learners can talk through emotional, behavioural or social difficulties with a trained adult. Counselling matters, but it cannot change everything around a child.

Some learners need confidential spaces to discuss grief, anxiety or family difficulties. But counselling usually responds after a problem has emerged and cannot, by itself, change the conditions contributing to that problem.

Our review showed that many of the pressures affecting children’s mental health – including bullying, violence, poverty, family stress and unsafe school environments – sit beyond what individual counselling can address. Counselling therefore needs to be combined with preventive, whole-school and community-linked approaches.

A school can have a counselling room and still be unsafe. It can have a guidance teacher and still tolerate bullying. It can teach learners to recognise depression and anxiety while having no way to get specialised care.

Role of teachers

Because specialist mental health professionals are scarce, many school-based programmes rely on task-sharing: training teachers and other non-specialists to take on defined mental health support roles. They can help create supportive environments, recognise signs of distress, reduce stigma and guide learners towards appropriate help.

But there must be boundaries. Teachers should not be expected to diagnose mental health conditions, manage serious cases or become substitute psychologists. Evidence from task-sharing programmes in low- and middle-income countries shows that non-specialists are most effective when their roles are clearly defined and supported by training, supervision and referral pathways to more specialised care, as well as clear procedures for confidentiality, safeguarding and referral.

Teacher well-being also matters. Adding mental health responsibilities without time, resources and support risks increasing workload and stress.

Beyond the school gate

Evidence from low- and middle-income countries shows that children’s mental health is shaped not only by what happens at school, but also by family, community and wider social conditions. Reviews of community- and family-based approaches show that involving caregivers, trusted community actors and referral services is valuable.

Schools cannot address children’s mental health alone. Parents and caregivers need support to recognise distress and follow through on referrals. Non-teaching staff also matter because learners may first confide in another trusted adult.

Schools need functioning links with health facilities, child-protection services, community organisations and social protection systems.

Across the studies we reviewed, implementation repeatedly depended on school leadership, cultural adaptation, financing, confidentiality, safeguarding, supervision, clear referral pathways and coordination across sectors.

Schools need mental health systems, not isolated services

Our review showed that isolated interventions are unlikely to be enough. Effective school mental health depends on the wider system around them, including leadership, trained staff, supervision, safeguarding, referral pathways, family engagement, teacher well-being, coordination with health and social services, and sustainable financing.

Charity Waweru-Mwangi contributed to this article.

articles.title: Childhood adversity linked to billions in health and economic costs – new research
articles.author: Kat Ford, Research Fellow in the Public Health Collaborating Unit, Bangor University; Liverpool John Moores University
articles.summary: The health effects of childhood adversity carry a huge economic burden, according to new research across Wales and England.
articles.contentHtml:
Childhood trauma can leave scars that last long after the experiences themselves have ended. Its effects can reach into adult life, increasing the risk of mental illness, physical health problems and other difficulties.

Our latest research estimates that the health effects associated with adverse childhood experiences cost the equivalent of £7.8 billion in Wales and £115.6 billion in England in 2023. These figures represent 8.4% of Wales’s gross domestic product (GDP) and 5% of England’s.

These are not bills paid directly by governments. Instead, they put a monetary value on the burden of illness and premature death associated with childhood adversity, showing the scale of its potential effects on society.

Adverse childhood experiences are traumatic or highly stressful events. They include physical, verbal and sexual abuse, as well as experiences such as domestic violence, parental separation, or living with a family member who has mental health problems, misuses alcohol or drugs, or has been in prison.

Around half of adults in England and Wales report at least one such experience. About one in ten report four or more.

Research has consistently linked childhood adversity to poorer health and wellbeing in adulthood. People exposed to several types of adversity face greater risks of mental illness, chronic physical conditions and health-harming behaviour, like smoking and harmful alcohol use. Childhood adversity has also been linked to poorer education and employment outcomes and a greater likelihood of involvement in violence.

These consequences can increase demand for healthcare and other public services. Understanding the costs helps to show the scale of the problem and the potential benefits of investing in prevention.

Counting the costs

We combined data from 10 studies conducted across England and Wales between 2012 and 2024. These studies interviewed adults about their childhood experiences and their health as adults. In total, we analysed data from 28,449 adults.

We examined seven causes of ill health, including mental illness, cancer, heart disease and stroke, alongside four health risks: smoking, high alcohol use, drug use and high body mass index. We explored links between childhood adversity and these outcomes, then used data from the global burden of disease study to estimate how much illness and premature death across the population could be associated with it.

Finally, we assigned a monetary value to these health effects using a government estimate of society’s willingness to pay to reduce ill health and premature death.

Read more: Childhood trauma linked to distrust of healthcare professionals – new research

Drug use and violence showed some of the strongest links with childhood adversity. Our estimates suggest it was associated with around 60% of drug use in Wales and 57% in England. It was also associated with almost half of all violence: 49% in Wales and 46% in England.

However, the largest estimated financial costs came from mental illness and smoking. This is because these affect more people and account for a greater share of ill health overall.

In Wales, the estimated costs associated with childhood adversity were £1.8 billion for mental illness and £1.8 billion for smoking. In England, the figures were £37.8 billion and £22.7 billion respectively.

We also calculated regional estimates for England for the first time. These ranged from £6.3 billion in the north east to £18 billion in the south east.

Why prevention matters

Our findings strengthen the case for preventing childhood adversity and supporting children and families who experience it. Reducing exposure to trauma could help improve health across people’s lives, while potentially reducing the wider costs associated with illness and premature death.

There are several ways to help prevent childhood adversity. These include supporting parents, building life skills, challenging harmful social norms and addressing the social conditions that put families under pressure.

Awareness and action to address childhood adversity has increased across the UK. Evidence suggests that some adverse childhood experiences may be declining. But others such as verbal abuse and household mental illness have been less addressed and may even be increasing.

People affected by trauma also need effective support. Trauma-informed approaches, which recognise how past experiences can shape people’s needs and behaviour, are one way to improve that support. For example, the Trauma-informed Wales Framework sets out an approach to understanding and responding to trauma across society.

Read more: The consequences of childhood trauma on children’s mental health

There are important limits to our findings. The estimates put a monetary value on health effects, including the value society places on reducing the risk of illness and premature death. They are not a direct measure of public spending or money that could automatically be saved through prevention. The study also identifies associations between childhood adversity and health outcomes, rather than proving that adversity caused every case.

Some vulnerable groups, including people in prison, were not represented in the surveys, despite being more likely to have experienced childhood adversity. Our estimates may therefore understate the true scale of the problem.

Even with these limitations, the findings highlight the potential scale of the health and economic burden associated with childhood adversity. Preventing trauma and providing better support for those affected could bring benefits that extend well beyond childhood.
